title: Feedback Modalities
subtitle: Visual, auditory, tactile and game-based feedback
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating feedback modalities within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain feedback modalities without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in feedback modalities.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to feedback modalities.

sections.explainSimply: Feedback can be a tone, animation, video brightness, game movement or another signal the learner can perceive.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Modality should match sensory needs, age, goals and tolerance. Highly stimulating feedback may improve engagement while also increasing arousal or masking fatigue.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Feedback design affects reward salience, cognitive load and attribution. Virtual-reality systems add immersion but may add cybersickness and attentional demands.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A driving instructor who gives immediate dashboard feedback while the learner practises a controllable skill.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand feedback modalities to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: The most entertaining feedback is not automatically the most therapeutic.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using feedback modalities predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: The most entertaining feedback is not automatically the most therapeutic. Evidence classification: practitioner consensus; limited comparative evidence.
